title: House GOP Faces Critical Test on Stopgap Funding and Defense Bills Before August Recess
excerpt: Senate Majority Leader Thune warns securing 50 votes for a $95 billion reconciliation package will be 'easier said than done' as both chambers race a packed legislative calendar.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • House Republicans are voting on a $1.15 trillion defense bill and a $95 billion budget resolution.
  • Speaker Johnson can lose only two Republican votes, with dissent already emerging.
  • Senate Majority Leader Thune doubts the Senate can pass the reconciliation package before recess.
  • Congress aims to avoid a third government shutdown ahead of the November midterms.
  • Urgency for a continuing resolution is heightened by past record-breaking government shutdowns.
House's Legislative Challenge
218

212

Funding Deadline (Dec 4)
  • House Republicans are voting Tuesday to open debate on a continuing resolution funding the government through December 4, a $1.15 trillion defense policy bill, and a $95 billion budget resolution.
  • Speaker Johnson can afford to lose no more than two Republican votes, and at least one member has already announced he will vote no.
  • Senate Majority Leader Thune has cast doubt on the Senate's ability to pass the reconciliation package before its August 6 departure, calling Johnson's timeline "news to me."
  • Congress has already weathered two record-breaking government shutdowns under Trump's second term, and Republicans are eager to avoid a third ahead of November midterm elections.

House Republican leaders face a defining legislative test on Tuesday as they attempt to advance a stopgap government funding bill, a sweeping defense authorization package, and a $95 billion budget resolution before the chamber departs for a five-week August recess on Thursday.

Lawmakers are slated to hold an afternoon vote to open debate on several measures including a continuing resolution that would fund federal agencies through December 4, the $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, and a budget resolution that would unlock a partisan reconciliation bill carrying $72 billion for defense and intelligence tied to the Iran war, $12 billion in farm aid, and $10 billion for Trump's SAVE America Act voter ID provisions, according to Reuters.

A Razor-Thin Margin

Speaker Mike Johnson's 218-212 seat majority leaves virtually no room for error. He can afford to lose no more than two Republican votes, with Democrats expected to oppose the measures unanimously. Republican hardliners have already blocked floor legislation three times since late June, including the defense policy bill.

https://x.com/foxnewspolitics/status/2079492016019484959 > **"We almost always get our work done," Representative Dusty Johnson told reporters.

"We've got to figure out how to get 50 votes for it."**

Representative Thomas Massie has announced he will vote against the procedural step, and at least three others remain undecided. "Confidence is an awfully strong word. This is the House Republicans. We almost always get our work done," Representative Dusty Johnson told reporters.

"We've got to figure out how to get 50 votes for it. That will be easier said than done."

— John Thune, Senate Majority Leader

Thune Pours Cold Water on Senate Timeline

Even if the House clears its agenda, the Senate presents a separate obstacle. Majority Leader John Thune has publicly questioned Johnson's ambition to pass the full reconciliation package before both chambers recess. When Johnson said both chambers would get it through, Thune told reporters it was "news to me," according to the Daily Caller.

The Senate's path is further complicated by the death of Budget Committee Chairman Lindsey Graham. Senator Ron Johnson of Wisconsin is expected to take over the committee, but no formal announcement has been made.

The SAVE America Act faces additional hurdles in the upper chamber. Thune has refused Trump's calls to fire Senate parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough, saying the legislation's fate is a "function of math." Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina has separately threatened to stall the bill, the Washington Examiner reported.

Shutdown Fears Drive the CR

Senate's Reconciliation Roadblocks
›Thune questions timeline for passing reconciliation package.
›Senate faces leadership changes with Graham's passing.
›Thune refuses to fire parliamentarian over legislative hurdles.
›Tillis threatens to stall the bill.

The urgency around the continuing resolution is driven by political math as much as fiscal necessity. Congress has endured two record-breaking government shutdowns since the start of Trump's second term — a 43-day full shutdown that ended last November and a 76-day partial shutdown that concluded in April.

Republicans are determined to avoid a repeat before November. "It takes away the leverage point for midterms to shut down the government," Representative Rich McCormick told the Washington Examiner.

Democrats have signaled opposition to the CR over language that could allow the transfer of Customs and Border Protection funds. House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar said he would vote against the measure, citing "drafting errors" that give CBP "flexibility to move money around."

Defense Funding Crunch

Pentagon officials have warned that defense funding could run dry by mid-August without congressional action. The reconciliation package's $72 billion for defense and intelligence is meant to address munitions shortfalls from the Iran conflict. But fiscal hawks object because it includes no spending offsets, and defense hawks argue the allocation falls short of Trump's call for $350 billion over a decade.

"If we don't get this done, we're gonna have to stay."

— Rick Scott, U.S. Senator (R-FL)
Shutdown History Fuels Urgency
›Congress experienced a 43-day shutdown last November.
›A 76-day partial shutdown ended in April.
›Republicans aim to avoid shutdown before November elections.
›Democrats oppose CR over Customs and Border Protection funding.

What to Watch

Tuesday's procedural vote will determine whether the House can begin floor debate. If it passes, the CR and NDAA could clear the House before Thursday's recess deadline, with the budget resolution vote expected Wednesday. The Senate's August 6 departure leaves a narrow window — and Thune's skepticism suggests a summer of uncertainty for government operations, defense readiness, and federal services including immigration processing.
